name: Aranmula Kannadi
tagline: Handmade metal mirror — a classic ashtamangalyam wedding gift from Aranmula
summary: Aranmula Kannadi is a handmade, first-surface metal mirror made in Aranmula (Pathanamthitta). It is one of the classical ashtamangalyam items used in Malayali weddings and a sought-after artisan gift.
description: Aranmula Kannadi is a handcrafted metal-alloy mirror made in the temple village of Aranmula on the banks of the Pamba river. The mirror is a first-surface metal mirror (the image forms on the polished metal surface itself) and is produced by a small number of traditional artisan families.

The mirror carries strong cultural value: it forms one of the eight auspicious items (ashtamangalyam) that appear in traditional Kerala wedding rituals and bridal trousseaus. Families prize authentic Aranmula mirrors for ritual use, heirloom display and as distinctive wedding gifts.

For visitors, the mirror offers a compact way to connect with Kerala’s living craft traditions: you can see the unique lost-wax/clay-mould casting and long polishing techniques, buy a genuine piece from a workshop or authorised outlet, and learn about the craft’s temple links and GI protection.
The craft receives formal recognition and promotion from state tourism and heritage organisations; genuine pieces are still made by a handful of households in and around Aranmula and nearby villages.
highlights: One of the eight ashtamangalyam items in Malayali weddings
Handmade first-surface metal mirror — no glass backing
Craft secrets passed in a few artisan families in Aranmula
Protected and promoted as a distinctive Kerala heritage craft
Available as small handheld 'vaalkannadi' or larger wall mirrors

sections.heading: Background
body: Aranmula Kannadi is a centuries-old metal-mirror tradition centred on Aranmula village in Pathanamthitta district. The craft is historically linked with the Aranmula Parthasarathy Temple and with hereditary metalworking families who conserve the alloy recipe, moulding and polishing skills.

The mirror is made from a copper–tin (bell-metal-like) alloy cast in clay moulds and then painstakingly polished to a reflective finish. Because the image forms on the polished metal surface itself (a first-surface mirror), Aranmula Kannadi gives a sharp, undistorted reflection distinct from ordinary backed glass mirrors.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Visit small family workshops in Aranmula to watch moulding, casting and finishing — craftsmen use traditional clay moulds, crucibles and multi-stage polishing to bring the metal to mirror finish. Workshop visits are short, tactile and well suited to travellers who want a close look at living craft techniques.

Buy an Aranmula Kannadi as a wedding gift or keepsake: mirrors come in a range of sizes from tiny handheld vaalkannadi to larger decorative wall mirrors. Ask for the maker’s name or family, confirm the piece is made in Aranmula, and prefer authorised outlets or direct purchases from recognised artisan families to avoid copies.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Aranmula is a short road journey from towns in central Travancore; visitors typically approach by road from Thiruvalla or Chengannur and from larger hubs such as Kottayam, Kochi (Cochin) or Thiruvananthapuram. Confirm local directions and transport options before you travel.

Workshops and emporia have informal visiting hours — phone ahead if you can, buy directly from artisans when possible, and pack mirrors carefully for transport. If you plan to present a mirror in a wedding ashtamangalyam, tell the artisan so you can choose an appropriate size and frame or mounting.

latest.text: Kerala Tourism features Aranmula Kannadi in its heritage and Kerala365 campaign pages, highlighting the craft as a visitor-interest tradition of Pathanamthitta.
The application for Geographical Indication (GI) for 'Aranmula Kannadi' is recorded in the early GI registry filings; the craft is recognised among the early GI-tagged Kerala handicrafts.

visitorInfo.bestTime: Year-round; festivals and Onam season bring more activity (boat race and temple events in Sep–Oct area).
visitorInfo.howToReach: Aranmula is in Pathanamthitta district on the Pamba river. Reach by road from Thiruvalla/Chengannur (nearest railheads) and by bus or car from Kottayam, Kochi or Thiruvananthapuram; confirm local transport options before travel.
etiquette: Buy from recognised artisan families or authorised outlets and ask about maker/family to ensure authenticity.
Ask for careful packing — mirrors are metal but reflective surfaces scratch; request soft wrapping and shell packing for flights.
If you plan to present it as an ashtamangalyam/wedding gift, tell the artisan so they can advise size and mounting.
Respect workshop etiquette: ask before photographing, wear clean shoes, and avoid touching polished surfaces.
